pioneers.evidence: She was the first female president of the ACM, from 1974 to 1976.

pioneers.name: Evelyn Berezin
pioneers.what: She led logic design on the Reservisor, an early airline reservation system for United Airlines. In 1969 she founded Redactron to sell her Data Secretary word processor.
pioneers.fact: Her Data Secretary word processor was about the size of a small refrigerator.
pioneers.evidence: She created the first computerized word processor and dubbed it the Data Secretary.

pioneers.name: Carol Shaw
pioneers.what: At Atari she designed 3-D Tic-Tac-Toe and Video Checkers for the 2600. At Activision she created River Raid (1982), a major hit vertically scrolling shooter.
pioneers.fact: Her first Atari project was a promo game tied to a Ralph Lauren cologne. Atari never published it.
pioneers.evidence: She is best known for creating the Atari 2600 vertically scrolling shooter game River Raid (1982) for Activision.

pioneers.name: Joan Clarke
pioneers.what: An English cryptanalyst in Bletchley Park's Hut 8, she worked on breaking German naval Enigma messages. She became deputy head of Hut 8 in 1944.
pioneers.fact: To be paid for a promotion she was classed as a linguist, and enjoyed writing 'languages: none' on forms.
pioneers.evidence: Clarke became deputy head of Hut 8 in 1944, although she was prevented from progressing because she was female

pioneers.name: Christopher Strachey
pioneers.what: A British pioneer of programming language design, he helped found denotational semantics and created CPL, an early influence on C. His 1951–52 draughts program may be the first video game.
pioneers.fact: In 1952 he programmed a love letter generator, called the first example of computer-generated literature.
pioneers.evidence: He created the programming language CPL, which was an early influence on C. He is credited as possibly the first developer of a video game

pioneers.name: Kateryna Yushchenko
pioneers.what: A Ukrainian computer scientist, in 1955 she created the Address programming language, an early high-level language using indirect addressing, akin to pointers.
pioneers.fact: Over her academic career she supervised 47 PhD students.
pioneers.evidence: She developed one of the world's first high-level languages with indirect address in programming (Pointers are analogous to this addressing), called the Address programming language.

pioneers.name: Anita Borg
pioneers.what: In 1987 she founded Systers, the first email network for women in technology. In 1994 she co-founded the Grace Hopper Celebration of Women in Computing.
pioneers.fact: Protests begun on her Systers list helped get Mattel to drop a Barbie doll's 'math class is tough' phrase.
pioneers.evidence: In 1987, Borg founded Systers, the first email network for women in technology.

pioneers.name: Adele Goldberg
pioneers.what: At Xerox PARC she co-developed Smalltalk-80, an early object-oriented language that influenced Python, Objective-C and Java. She was ACM president from 1984 to 1986.
pioneers.fact: With Alan Kay she described the Dynabook, a portable personal computer, in the 1976 article 'Personal Dynamic Media'.
pioneers.evidence: She was a co-developer of the programming language Smalltalk-80, an early object-oriented programming language that influenced the design of languages such as Python, Objective-C, and Java

pioneers.name: Susan Kare
pioneers.what: An artist, she designed icons and typefaces for the original Apple Macintosh, including the Chicago font. She later designed the card deck for Windows 3.0 Solitaire.
pioneers.fact: She sketched her first Mac icons in a $2.50 notebook of the smallest graph paper she could find.
pioneers.evidence: contributed interface elements and typefaces for the first Apple Macintosh personal computer from 1983 to 1986

pioneers.name: Karen Spärck Jones
pioneers.what: A self-taught British programmer, she introduced inverse document frequency (IDF) in a 1972 paper. IDF weighting underlies most modern search engines.
pioneers.fact: Her slogan was 'Computing is too important to be left to men.'
pioneers.evidence: responsible for the concept of inverse document frequency (IDF), a technology that underlies most modern search engines

pioneers.name: Barbara Liskov
pioneers.what: She introduced abstract data types and the Liskov substitution principle, and designed the CLU and Argus languages. She won the 2008 Turing Award.
pioneers.fact: Her PhD thesis was a chess endgame program, for which she developed the killer heuristic.
pioneers.evidence: Her notable work includes the introduction of abstract data types and the accompanying principle of data abstraction, along with the Liskov substitution principle

pioneers.name: Shafi Goldwasser
pioneers.what: With Silvio Micali she introduced probabilistic encryption, and with Micali and Charles Rackoff, zero-knowledge proofs. She shared the 2012 Turing Award.
pioneers.fact: She is a lead on Project CETI, an effort to translate the communication of sperm whales.
pioneers.evidence: In 1985, Goldwasser, Silvio Micali, and Charles Rackoff introduced zero-knowledge proofs

pioneers.name: Elizabeth "Jake" Feinler
pioneers.what: She directed the ARPANET's Network Information Center at SRI. Her group created the WHOIS directory and the top-level domain convention (.com, .org, .gov).
pioneers.fact: Her nickname 'Jake' came from her toddler sister saying 'Betty Jo' as 'Baby Jake'.
pioneers.evidence: she and her team created the Host Naming Registry (WHOIS) and the top-level domain naming convention (.com, .gov, .org… etc)

pioneers.name: Dame Stephanie "Steve" Shirley
pioneers.what: A Kindertransport child refugee, she founded Freelance Programmers with £6, hiring mostly women working part time from home. Her team programmed Concorde's black box.
pioneers.fact: She signed letters 'Steve' because company letters signed with her real name went unanswered.
pioneers.evidence: Shirley founded the software company Freelance Programmers with a capital of £6.

pioneers.name: Danielle Bunten Berry
pioneers.what: She designed M.U.L.E. (1983), one of the first influential multiplayer video games, and The Seven Cities of Gold. Ten of her 12 games were built around multiplayer.
pioneers.fact: Her first game, a 1978 Apple II auction game called Wheeler Dealers, sold only 50 copies.
pioneers.evidence: known for the 1983 game M.U.L.E., one of the first influential multiplayer video games, and 1984's The Seven Cities of Gold

pioneers.name: Mary Ann Horton
pioneers.what: A Usenet and Internet pioneer, she worked on Berkeley UNIX and vi, created uuencode for binary email attachments, and led Usenet's growth in the 1980s.
pioneers.fact: In 1997 she got Lucent to become the first large company with transgender-inclusive equal opportunity language.
pioneers.evidence: created the first email binary attachment tool uuencode, and led the growth of Usenet in the 1980s

pioneers.name: Sophie Germain
pioneers.what: French mathematician and physicist, one of the pioneers of elasticity theory. She won the Paris Academy of Sciences grand prize, and her work on Fermat's Last Theorem shaped the field for centuries.
pioneers.fact: She wrote to Lagrange, Legendre and Gauss under the pen name Monsieur Le Blanc, borrowed from a former student.
pioneers.evidence: correspondence under the pseudonym of Monsieur Le Blanc with famous mathematicians, such as Lagrange, Legendre, and Gauss

pioneers.name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
pioneers.what: American astronomer who worked at Harvard College Observatory. She found the period-luminosity relation of Cepheid variable stars, giving astronomers the first standard candle for measuring distances to other galaxies.
pioneers.fact: Leavitt was deaf; asteroid 5383 Leavitt and a Moon crater honor her and other deaf astronomers.
pioneers.evidence: The asteroid 5383 Leavitt and the crater Leavitt on the Moon are named after her to honor deaf men and women who have worked as astronomers.

pioneers.name: Lise Meitner
pioneers.what: Austrian-Swedish nuclear physicist who, with her nephew Otto Frisch, worked out the physics of nuclear fission in 1938. She was the first woman to become a full professor of physics in Germany.
pioneers.fact: Element 109, meitnerium, was named after her in 1997.
pioneers.evidence: In 1997, element 109 was named meitnerium.

pioneers.name: Emmy Noether
pioneers.what: German mathematician who helped build modern abstract algebra. Her theorems link symmetry to conservation laws, a cornerstone of mathematical physics.
pioneers.fact: An asteroid, 7001 Noether, is named after her, along with many mathematical objects.
pioneers.evidence: Several things now bear her name, including many mathematical objects, and an asteroid, 7001 Noether.

pioneers.name: Edith Clarke
pioneers.what: American electrical engineer who specialized in power system analysis. She was the first woman employed as an electrical engineer in the US and the first female professor of electrical engineering there.
pioneers.fact: She invented the Clarke calculator, an early graphing calculator for power-line equations, patented in 1925.
pioneers.evidence: she invented the Clarke calculator, an early graphing calculator

pioneers.name: Beatrice Shilling
pioneers.what: English aeronautical engineer who designed the RAE Restrictor in the Second World War. The simple device stopped Rolls-Royce Merlin engines losing power during negative-g manoeuvres.
pioneers.fact: She lapped the Brooklands circuit at over 100 mph on a motorcycle and later helped build an RAF Olympic bobsled.
pioneers.evidence: On 24 August 1934 she  lapped the Brooklands circuit at over 100 miles per hour

pioneers.name: Chien-Shiung Wu
pioneers.what: Chinese-American experimental physicist whose Wu experiment proved that parity is not conserved. She also worked on uranium isotope separation for the Manhattan Project.
pioneers.fact: She sewed her own qipao dresses and always wore one under her lab coat.
pioneers.evidence: buy fabric to make her own qipao, which she always wore under her lab coat

pioneers.name: Stephanie Kwolek
pioneers.what: Polish-American chemist at DuPont who invented Kevlar. She became the fourth woman added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame.
pioneers.fact: Kevlar came from a cloudy polymer solution, the kind that was usually thrown away.
pioneers.evidence: This sort of cloudy solution was usually thrown away.

pioneers.name: Daphne Oram
pioneers.what: British composer who co-founded the BBC Radiophonic Workshop. She created the Oramics technique for drawing sound, and was the first woman to design and build an electronic musical instrument.
pioneers.fact: She set up her own electronic music studio in Tower Folly, a converted oast house in Kent.
pioneers.evidence: established the Oramics Studios for Electronic Composition in Tower Folly, a converted oast house at Fairseat, Kent

pioneers.name: Vera Rubin
pioneers.what: American astronomer who studied how fast galaxies rotate. Her rotation-curve measurements were a key piece of evidence for dark matter.
pioneers.fact: Vera Rubin Ridge on Mars and asteroid 5726 Rubin are named after her.
pioneers.evidence: An area on Mars, Vera Rubin Ridge, is named after her, as well as the asteroid 5726 Rubin.

pioneers.name: Pauline Oliveros
pioneers.what: American composer and accordionist, a central figure in post-war experimental and electronic music. She co-founded and directed the San Francisco Tape Music Center and developed the idea of deep listening.
pioneers.fact: In 1987 she had her accordion retuned from equal temperament to just intonation.
pioneers.evidence: Oliveros was openly lesbian.

pioneers.name: Delia Derbyshire
pioneers.what: English composer at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop. Her 1963 electronic realisation of the Doctor Who theme was one of the first TV themes made entirely with electronics.
pioneers.fact: Hearing her version, composer Ron Grainer asked, "Did I really write this?" She replied, "Most of it."
pioneers.evidence: he asked: "Did I really write this?", to which Derbyshire replied: "Most of it".

pioneers.name: Valentina Tereshkova
pioneers.what: Soviet cosmonaut and engineer who became the first woman in space on Vostok 6 in 1963. She orbited Earth 48 times and is the only woman to fly a solo space mission.
pioneers.fact: Her call sign was Chaika (Seagull), and an asteroid, 1671 Chaika, was later named for it.
pioneers.evidence: Her call sign on this flight was Chaika.

pioneers.name: Patricia Bath
pioneers.what: American ophthalmologist who developed the laserphaco probe for safer, more precise cataract surgery. She was the first African-American woman doctor to receive a patent for a medical purpose.
pioneers.fact: She coined the term "laser phaco", short for laser photoablative cataract surgery.
pioneers.evidence: Bath coined the term "laser phaco" for the process, short for laser photoablative cataract surgery

pioneers.name: Jocelyn Bell Burnell
pioneers.what: Northern Irish astrophysicist who discovered the first pulsar in 1967 as a doctoral student. She gave her $3 million Breakthrough Prize to fund students from under-represented groups in physics.
pioneers.fact: The first pulsar was nicknamed "Little Green Man 1" and first showed up as a "bit of scruff" on chart paper.
pioneers.evidence: Temporarily dubbed "Little Green Man 1" (LGM-1)

pioneers.name: Laurie Spiegel
pioneers.what: American composer and software engineer who worked at Bell Labs. She created Music Mouse, an algorithmic "intelligent instrument" released in 1986.
pioneers.fact: Her version of Kepler's Harmonice Mundi is on the Voyager Golden Record, now heading out of the solar system.
pioneers.evidence: Spiegel's musical interpretation of Johannes Kepler's Harmonice Mundi appeared on the "Sounds of Earth" section of the Voyager Golden Record.

pioneers.name: Ben Barres
pioneers.what: American neurobiologist at Stanford who studied how glial cells interact with neurons. In 2013 he became the first openly transgender scientist in the National Academy of Sciences.
pioneers.fact: He left a neurology residency to research glial cells after spotting patterns in pathology reports.
pioneers.evidence: became the first openly transgender scientist in the National Academy of Sciences in 2013

pioneers.name: Mae Jemison
pioneers.what: American engineer, physician and NASA astronaut. In 1992 she became the first African-American woman in space, aboard Space Shuttle Endeavour.
pioneers.fact: She opened her shifts in orbit with "Hailing frequencies open" and later appeared on Star Trek: The Next Generation.
pioneers.evidence: she began communications on her shift with the salute "Hailing frequencies open", a quote from Star Trek.

pioneers.name: Ellen Ochoa
pioneers.what: American engineer and astronaut who became the first Latina in space in 1993. She later became the first Latina director of NASA's Johnson Space Center.
pioneers.fact: A classical flutist, she took a flute with her on her first mission to space.
pioneers.evidence: She took a flute with her on her first mission to space.

pioneers.name: Maryam Mirzakhani
pioneers.what: Iranian mathematician and Stanford professor who studied the geometry of Riemann surfaces. In 2014 she became the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal.
pioneers.fact: She solved problems by doodling on big sheets of paper; her daughter called her work "painting".
pioneers.evidence: To solve problems, Mirzakhani would draw doodles on sheets of paper and write mathematical formulas around the drawings.
